query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Inserting an ultrathin Cr-based interlayer into HEA multilayer coatings enhances interface coherency, thereby shifting the dominant creep mechanism from diffusion-mediated at high temperatures to dislocation-mediated under mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers without a dedicated transition layer, exhibiting a mixed creep behavior primarily governed by diffusion at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Integrate an ultrathin Cr-based interlayer with systematically varied thickness into the existing HEA multilayer stack.
generation.conditions: High-temperature creep testing under controlled mechanical loading, replicating service conditions typical for advanced coating applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The Cr-based interlayer promotes enhanced lattice coherency at the interfaces between HEA layers.
generation.mechanism: The ultrathin Cr interlayer reduces lattice mismatch, which can lower diffusion barriers and simultaneously modulate dislocation nucleation sites. This controlled adjustment in interfacial structure is expected to reduce diffusion creep tendencies and enable a transition to dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to HEA multilayers without the interlayer, the Cr-modified multilayers will show a measurable decrease in diffusion-controlled creep rates with an increase in dislocation activity, evidenced by changes in creep strain rates and dislocation densities.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers lacking the Cr-based interlayer, where diffusion-mediated creep predominates at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The observed effect is contingent upon achieving an optimal ultrathin Cr interlayer thickness; excessively thick layers could lead to unintended brittle phase formation or other adverse microstructural changes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise critical thickness for the Cr interlayer and the quantitative extent of the shift between creep mechanisms require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate multiple HEA multilayer samples with an integrated Cr-based interlayer at varying thicknesses (e.g., 1 nm, 5 nm, and 10 nm) alongside control samples without the interlayer. Subject all samples to identical high-temperature creep tests under controlled mechanical loading, then perform microstructural investigations using techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess dislocation density and interface coherency.
measurements: Creep strain rate under high-temperature conditions
Dislocation density and distribution via TEM
Microstructural characterization of interface coherency (using diffraction techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no systematic shift in creep behavior (i.e., no reduction in diffusion-mediated creep indicators or increase in dislocation activity) is observed as a function of Cr interlayer thickness compared to the control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

frame.system: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers used as advanced coatings, where the layers and their interfaces (with varying degrees of coherency) govern creep behavior.
frame.goal: To identify a material that can serve as an interlayer to promote and control the transition between diffusion-mediated creep and dislocation-mediated creep, thereby clarifying the role of interface coherency in the overall creep response.
frame.limitation: The specific impact of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers is not yet understood.
root_cause_cues: transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms
constraints: Material must be able to mediate a change in dominant creep mechanism
Must be compatible with HEA multilayer structures and coating applications
Should exhibit properties that favor both diffusion (at high temperatures) and dislocation activity (mechanical load accommodation)
frame.regime: High-temperature and mechanical stress conditions typical of creep testing in advanced coating applications, where both diffusion and dislocation processes may occur.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have explored HEA multilayers for superior mechanical and irradiation properties; however, they have not isolated or clearly defined the role of interface coherency in governing the creep behavior. This gap has left the mechanism for transitioning between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep unresolved.

decision.trend: Early studies in HEAs have largely concentrated on optimizing overall properties—such as strength, oxidation resistance, and deformation behavior—by tweaking compositions and processing routes (e.g., HPHT treatments, laser cladding). In doing so, researchers observed that engineered microstructural features (for instance, finely tuned phase distributions and coherent interfaces) can dramatically influence deformation modes. More recent work has begun to highlight that a very small lattice mismatch between adjacent phases (as seen when Cr addition promotes coherent B2 or other precipitates) not only improves strength and ductility but may also impact the operative creep mechanism. Despite these advances, none of the previous studies have isolated the specific role of a designed interlayer or transition material in prompting a switch between diffusional creep and dislocation creep in HEA multilayers.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved issue is how interface coherency—specifically through the deliberate introduction of an interlayer material—can serve to mediate a transition between diffusion-controlled creep at high temperatures and dislocation-mediated creep under mechanical loading. This gap lies in understanding the interplay between interfacial structure and the dual creep mechanisms in multilayer HEA coatings.
decision.lever: Integrate an ultrathin Cr-based interlayer with systematically varied thickness (and hence interfacial coherency) into the HEA multilayer stack
decision.why: Cr has been demonstrated in related studies to modulate lattice mismatch effectively, thereby enhancing interface coherency. Its ability to influence both atomic diffusion rates (facilitating diffusion creep at elevated temperatures) and dislocation nucleation/barrier properties (governing dislocation-mediated creep) makes it a promising candidate to bridge the two creep regimes and directly address the open question regarding the role of interface coherency in HEA multilayers.
